# The REPL, Then the Contract {#sec-repl}

The language definition describes the intended first experience in passing,
and it is the whole product philosophy:

> It is possible to get quite far using R interactively, executing simple
> expressions from the command line. Some users may never need to go beyond
> that level, others will want to write their own functions either in an ad
> hoc fashion to systematize repetitive work or with the perspective of
> writing add-on packages for new functionality.

That ladder --- expression, function, package --- is the honest path. It
is also why a person who wants illegal states to be unrepresentable feels
like they are fighting the grain. They are. The grain is a conversation.
Contracts are what you write down when the conversation has discovered a
thing worth keeping.

## What the conversation is good at

Interactive data work wants:

- load something real
- poke it
- draw it
- summarize it
- notice which poke you are about to repeat
- wrap the repetition in a function
- and, sometimes, put the function in a package so a stranger can call it

Features that serve that ladder are easy to mistake for sloppiness.
Promises let a plotting function capture the expression you wrote.
Attributes let a vector grow a class without a new runtime type. The
search path lets a new package's verbs appear in the conversation.
Recycling and permissive coercion let a one-liner survive contact with a
column that is *almost* the right shape. `NA` lets a summary skip missing
measurements without a parallel `Option` type. Non-standard evaluation
lets a modeling formula look like the thing a statistician would write on
paper.

Morandat and colleagues described this lifecycle as the context in which
the linguistic cocktail makes sense. Take the lifecycle away and a lot of
R looks indefensible. Leave it in place and the language looks like a
tool that knows what the first hour of analysis is.

## What the conversation will not do for you

The same features are anti-features for "schema at the boundary," until
you impose a discipline above the language.

A promise will evaluate in a surprising environment if you capture it and
force it later. A class attribute will be ignored by any function that is
not generic. The search path will resolve a name to whatever was attached
last. Coercion will add a factor level you did not mean, or drop one.
`NA` will flow through a logical test and return `NA`, and `if (NA)` will
complain, and somewhere in that pair of behaviors a bug will hide for a
year. None of this is a reason to refuse the REPL. It is a reason to
treat the REPL as the place you discover the concept, and the package as
the place you stop the concept from leaking.

The sequence that matches the ladder, said as advice:

1. Explore with the dynamic machine. Dirty data, wrong types, one-off
   plots, `inspect` when a result is absurd.
2. Notice the nouns that kept coming back, and the verbs you repeated.
3. Parse those nouns at the boundary. Constructors that refuse junk.
   `format` methods that make the meaning obvious.
4. Package the verbs. Generics where a stranger should be able to add a
   method. A handle only where identity is the feature.

Step 2 is the part people skip, and then step 3 becomes ceremony around
the wrong nouns. The low-level session this book came from was step 1
aimed at the language itself. That is allowed. Most days step 1 is aimed
at a file full of addresses.

## Why Python and JavaScript feel more direct

They default to named objects with methods. The habit "there is a class
for this" is ambient, so the path from a domain noun to a bundle of
behavior is short. You still do not get real contracts until you add
something like Pydantic or Zod. The object was never the contract. It was
a place to put methods. The contract arrives when construction parses.

R's ambient habit is "there is a function for this," and a class is
optional metadata on a vector. The path from a domain noun to a defended
value is longer, because you are building the noun out of a vector, a
class attribute, and a constructor the language considers optional. The
reward, when someone actually does it, is an API that composes. A request
is a value. A plot specification is a value. A data frame is a relation.
Verbs take these and return these. The user interface is the vocabulary.

This is a personal preference and also a technical one. Dislike of
message-passing as a default is compatible with respecting what that
default buys: one obvious place to look for behavior. R asks you to look
in the verbs, which is wonderful when the verbs are curated and miserable
when every package invents a private dialect. Curation is the price of
the preference. @sec-verbs is about paying it on purpose.

## Where R wins on the merits

A few comparisons, kept specific so they do not turn into team sports.

**httr2.** A request is a value you build with a pipe of functions:
URL, headers, body, authentication, then perform. The
[introductory vignette](https://httr2.r-lib.org/articles/httr2.html)
shows the shape. Errors are classed. The perform step is the edge where
the value meets the network. This is the functional core and the
imperative shell in one pipeline, and it is pleasant in a way
object-graphs of HTTP clients often are not. You can see the request. You
can print it before you send it. Printing is part of the design.

**ellmer.** A conversation with a model is a session you hold, and the
operations on it are a small vocabulary: send a turn, register a tool,
extract a typed value. The
[package site](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org/) is the reference. A
conversation has identity --- turns accumulate --- so a handle is the
honest representation. The design win over a large agent framework is the
size of the vocabulary and the refusal to hide the request. Compare that
with LangChain-style graphs when you want a lesson in what "more objects"
does to a domain that wanted a few verbs. The lesson is not that Python
cannot be clear. It is that a framework can spend its complexity budget
on the wrong axis.

**ggplot2.** Wilkinson's *Grammar of Graphics* gave the field a
vocabulary. Wickham's
[layered grammar](https://doi.org/10.1198/jcgs.2009.07098) turned it into
an embedded language of data, aesthetic mappings, geoms, stats, and
facets. You can dislike using it and still recognize the move. A plot is
a specification, a value, built by composing layers. It is not a scene
graph you mutate. Formulas in modeling packages are the older version of
the same move. R's frameworks, when they work, look like grammars.

**Tidy data and verbs.** Once a data frame is a relation with a
convention for rows and columns, a whole ecology of verbs can share it.
The win is the shared noun, not any single package. A new verb can be
written without inheriting from a table class. That is open dispatch as
an industry structure, and it is the subject of the next chapter.

## The nag

Python nags you early, with objects. You still need a schema library
before the nag means "invalid states are unrepresentable." R nags you
late, with `stopifnot` scattered through helpers and with users who
received a list and had to guess. Unless the package treats the contract
as the product.

The REPL is not a betrayal of that product. It is how you find out which
contracts are worth writing. The difficult part is that the language will
never force the transition. You can stay in the conversation forever.
Production R is the decision to leave the conversation in the places where
the concept has stabilized, and to keep the conversation available
everywhere it has not.
